children: By Al Root and Mariapaula Gonzalez
Thursday was a wild, somewhat confusing day for Corteva as it completed the spinoff of its agricultural seed technology business, Vylor.
The confusion-and the creation of two stand-alone companies-has created an opportunity for investors, according to early Wall Street opinions.

Corteva stock appeared to drop 84% to $12.57 on Thursday. The stock really wasn't down that much. Instead, the company split in two. Vylor, the old DuPont Pioneer seed business, is now a stand-alone company. Vylor stock didn't trade ahead of the spin, however, making Thursday a little nerve-racking for Corteva investors.

The investors got one share of Vylor for every share of Corteva, which kept its crop protection business. Vylor stock closed at $68.26. So with Corteva at $12.57, the combined value was $80.83. Corteva investors made money on the day.
Now, Wall Street will start weighing in on both stocks and their updated businesses. So far, Wall Street thinks both are attractive.
"The market is valuing Corteva like a no-growth commodity chemical [company]," wrote Morgan Stanley analyst Vincent Andrews on Friday. "Proprietary R&D pipeline work suggests the opposite."

To be sure, some insecticides and herbicides are commodities, but Corteva invests in new formulations and products that can provide growth and margin stability. He rates shares Buy and has an $18 price target for the new stock, up almost 50% from recent levels.
His target values Corteva at about 18.5 times his 2027 estimated earnings per share of 97 cents. That's in line with the S&P 500 multiple.

As for Vylor, Andrews sees Vylor as a key player in the seed and biotech market alongside peer Bayer (which owns Vylor competitor Monsanto), primarily in corn and soybean production. He rates shares Buy and has a $85 price target.

Seeds these days have a lot of embedded genetic technology, providing pricing power and licensing opportunities. RBC analyst Arun Viswanathan also launched coverage on Vylor stock with a Buy rating and $85 price target. He called the company a "double-digit percent earnings per share compounder," adding "elite genetics" drive mid-single-digit percentage long-term sales growth.
Good seed genetics essentially translates into big crop yields.
His target implies Vylor should trade for 34 times his 2027 earnings per share estimate. He projects about 12% annual earnings per share growth between 2026 and 2028.
Vylor stock was down 2.3% on Friday at $66.72, while the S&P 500 was up 1%. Corteva shares were up 3.3% at $12.98.
